The men eat 30000 kg a day. The horses eat 90000 kg — three times as much. Together the army consumes 120 tonnes of food and fodder every single day.

That ratio is the secret history of pre-modern warfare: the army's stomach was mostly animal. Cavalry, draught teams, and pack animals multiplied a force's mobility and multiplied its appetite faster. And supply wagons make the problem recursive — a wagon carrying fodder is pulled by horses that eat fodder, so beyond a certain distance from the magazine, a wagon train delivers nothing net at all: the team consumes the cargo en route. This is why the effective radius of operations from a supply base was so short, why campaigns clung to navigable rivers where barges could carry bulk, and why commanders timed offensives for just after the harvest, when the army could eat the countryside it marched through.

The numbers also explain the strategy of devastation. Burning an enemy's crops and mills was not vandalism; it was arithmetic warfare — deleting 120-tonne-days of supply from the board before the enemy army arrived to need them. Battles decided campaigns in the chronicles. Fodder decided them in fact.
Why did pre-modern campaigns so often follow rivers, and start after the harvest? It sounds like a scheduling quirk.

It is logistics wearing a calendar. An army consumes food and fodder in tonnage that land transport could barely move: a wagon on a pre-modern road carried perhaps half a tonne, drawn by animals that themselves ate into the load. Water transport broke the equation — a single river barge carried what dozens of wagons did, and its draught animals (or the current) didn't consume the cargo. The cost schedules preserved in Diocletian's price edict are often used to estimate the ratio: moving goods by sea was cheapest by far, river transport cost several times more, and road haulage cost many times more again — orders of magnitude apart, though the exact figures depend on how you read the edict. So armies campaigned along the Danube, the Rhine, the Po, the great river roads of China, and supplied themselves from floating magazines wherever they could.

The harvest set the other boundary. An army living substantially off the land — which most did, whatever their supply train — needed the crops standing or just gathered: march too early and the fields are green and ungathered; too late and the peasants have hidden or consumed the surplus and winter is closing the roads. The campaigning season from late spring to autumn, conventional across Europe and much of Asia, is the harvest cycle plus the weather. It also fitted the agricultural labor cycle: soldiers who were farmers could be spared, if at all, in that same window.

Read old campaigns with this in mind and their shapes stop looking arbitrary. The route hugging a river, the pause at a fortress town with magazines, the retreat when the country is 'eaten out' — these are supply decisions. Strategy in the chronicles is written as the clash of wills; on the ground it was the clash of appetites with geography.

A siege is often described as a starvation contest. Quantify one side of it: a besieged city of 50000 people is rationed to 0.6 kg of grain per person per day, and its storehouses hold 1800 tonnes of grain. How long does the city hold out on grain alone? And what decides the other side's clock?
The city's daily grain consumption, in tonnes:
Days the storehouses last at that ration:

The city burns 30 tonnes of grain a day, so its stores last 60 days — two months, if rationing starts at once, if the stores are honestly counted, if nothing burns, spoils, or is stolen, and if grain were the whole of diet, which it never quite is.

Every siege is two such clocks racing. The besieger's clock is set by his own supply problem, usually worse than the defender's: his army is camped in a countryside it has already eaten bare, supplied over lengthening lines, rotting in its own camp diseases — besieging armies routinely lost more men to dysentery than to the walls. The defender's clock is the storehouse; the attacker's clock is the forage radius and the season. Storming the walls is what a commander does when his clock is shorter: assault trades men's lives for time. Starving a city out is what he does when his clock is longer and he can afford to let arithmetic fight for him.

Hence the obsessive importance, on the defense, of the pre-siege decisions: expelling 'useless mouths' — a real and brutal technical term of siegecraft — driving in the countryside's livestock and harvest before the ring closed, and filling the cisterns. And on the attacker's side, the decisive weapon was often the blockade of the harbor or river that fed the city. Constantinople survived a dozen sieges behind its sea supply; it fell in 1453 when the sea side was finally closed too. The walls get the paintings. The granaries decided.
Castles went from tall stone keeps to those low, star-shaped fortresses in a couple of centuries. What forced the redesign?

Gunpowder artillery, and specifically the demonstration — most famously during the French invasion of Italy in 1494 — that a mobile siege train could batter a medieval curtain wall to rubble in days rather than months. The medieval wall was tall and thin: height defeated ladders and gave defenders plunging fire, but a tall thin wall is exactly what a cannonball wants to meet — it cracks, it sheds fatal splinters of stone, and its own height makes its fall catastrophic. The geometry of defense had to invert.

The answer, developed in Italy and exported everywhere — the trace italienne, the star fort — follows from three requirements. First, thickness and lowness: walls became low, massively thick, and backed with earth, which absorbs shot instead of shattering. Second, the elimination of dead ground: the angular bastion — the arrowhead of masonry projecting at each corner — lets defenders fire along the face of the neighboring wall, so there is no spot at the wall's base where an attacker can work unshot at. The star shape is not decoration; it is interlocking fields of fire drawn in plan view. Third, defense in depth: ravelins, covered ways, and a sloped glacis that exposes attackers while hiding the wall's base from direct fire.

The cost was staggering — a star fortress cost many times a castle and needed a garrison and guns to match — which had a political consequence: only states, not lords, could build them. Fortification followed artillery into the hands of central governments, and the military map of Europe simplified into states that could afford the geometry and places that could not.
What was the difference between a feudal levy and a professional army, in terms of how the system actually worked?

The levy is an obligation denominated in time. Under classic feudal arrangements, land was held in return for military service — a vassal owed his lord a period of service with his own equipment and retinue, conventionally around forty days in many medieval European customs, though the terms varied by place and period. The system needed no treasury: the army paid itself, in land held long-term. Its defects were built into the denomination. Forty days is barely time to assemble, march, and begin a siege. The service expired on schedule regardless of the campaign's state — commanders watched armies legally dissolve mid-operation. And the men owed harvest-season duties at home that pulled the same way.

The escape routes all run through money. Scutage — 'shield money' — let a vassal pay cash instead of serving, and let the king hire soldiers who served as long as they were paid. Mercenary companies, paid retinues under written indentures, and eventually standing armies are the levy progressively converted into a payroll. Professional soldiers brought what the levy never could: year-round availability, standardized training and equipment, and obedience to the paymaster rather than to local obligation.

But the conversion had a price that reshaped states. A standing army is a permanent expense of enormous size, and paying it required permanent taxation, a treasury, borrowing — in short, the fiscal state. This is the sense of the famous aphorism that war made the state: rulers who wanted professional force had to build tax machines, and the tax machines outlasted the wars. The levy asked landholders for days; the professional army asked whole societies for money, forever.
On land, armies are limited by food and fodder. What limited navies in the age of sail — what ran out first?

Water. A ship can carry months of salt pork and biscuit, and it can catch fish and rain, but fresh water is heavy, bulky, goes stale in the cask, and is consumed at an unbudgeable rate by every man aboard every day. A warship with several hundred men measured its endurance in weeks of water, not months of food. This is why the strategic map of the sailing era is a map of watering places: fleets clung to coasts and islands, campaigns were choreographed around springs and rivers, and a navy without forward bases was a navy with short arms. Control of a harbor with good water was a military asset of the first rank.

The second limit was slower and crueller: scurvy. On long voyages without fresh provisions, crews were progressively disabled by vitamin C deficiency — on some famous voyages, the majority of the crew died of it. Anson's circumnavigation in the 1740s lost well over half its men, mostly to scurvy. The empirical fix existed — citrus juice — and James Lind's controlled comparison of treatments in 1753 is a landmark in medical method; yet the Royal Navy did not mandate lemon juice until 1795, a lag of four decades between demonstration and institution that cost uncounted lives. When it did, British fleets could stay at sea on blockade for months, a strategic transformation purchased with fruit juice.

Wood, cordage, and sailcloth wore out too, and hulls fouled and rotted — a fleet was a wasting asset even in peacetime. But water set the radius and scurvy set the clock; everything else about naval strategy in the period is commentary on those two constraints.

How fast could news travel before the telegraph? Compare two systems for me: a single rider who has to rest his horse, managing about 60 km a day, versus a relay system where fresh horses are staged along the road and the message keeps moving 10 hours a day at an average of 15 km/h. What does the relay deliver per day, and how many times faster is it?

The relay's advantage over the lone rider:

The relay moves the message 150 km a day — 2.5 times the lone rider's pace.

That multiplier is why every large empire built the same machine: staged posts with fresh horses, riders, and fodder waiting, from the Persian royal road system — Herodotus' line about couriers stopped by 'neither snow nor rain nor heat nor night,' later borrowed as the American postal motto, described these riders — to the Roman cursus publicus, the Mongol yam, and the Inca chasqui runners who relayed messages (and fresh fish for the emperor's table) across the Andes on foot. The technology is not the horse; it is the organization: stations at intervals, maintained at state expense, with the cost justified because orders, tax reports, and news of revolt were the empire's nervous system.

Notice what the relay does not do: it does not scale. A relay carries a letter, not a newspaper; bandwidth stayed near zero even as speed improved. And it was ruinously expensive per message, reserved for the state's own traffic — private letters moved at merchant speed, with caravans and ships, which is to say weeks behind events. The pre-telegraph world therefore had a strange information geography: governments might learn of a frontier revolt in days, while the public learned of it in a month, and prices in a port city moved on news that was old before it was written down. The telegraph did not just speed news up; it democratized the speed, and that was the revolution.
There's a famous line that 'war made the state.' That sounds backwards — surely states make war?

The line is Charles Tilly's, and the full version runs: 'War made the state, and the state made war.' His argument is about selection pressure. Between about 990 and 1990, Europe went from several hundred independent political units to a few dozen — the ones that survived were, disproportionately, the ones that got good at extracting resources for war. Rulers who wanted to fight needed soldiers; soldiers needed pay, food, and weapons; those needed taxes, loans, and officials to collect and account for them. Each round of military competition forced administrative growth: treasuries, tax surveys, debt instruments, professional bureaucracies. Rulers who failed to build the extraction machine were conquered by rulers who had — so the map selected for fiscal capacity the way an environment selects for camouflage.

Tilly also distinguished paths. Where cities and capital were dense (the Dutch Republic, Venice), rulers bargained with merchants and built capital-intensive states. Where land and peasants dominated (Russia, Brandenburg), they coerced labor directly and built coercion-intensive states. Where both existed (France, England), the balanced 'capitalized coercion' path produced the strongest competitors. The modern national state, in his telling, is what you get when all three paths are run through a thousand years of military elimination.

It is a thesis, not a law — it fits Europe better than everywhere, and critics note it underplays trade, religion, and law as state-builders. But it permanently changed the question. Before Tilly, the tax office looked like a support function for the army. After Tilly, the army looks like the selection pressure that explains the tax office.
Generals talk about 'living off the land' versus supplying from magazines. What was the real trade-off?

It is a trade between speed and certainty, and both sides of it are arithmetic. A magazine system — supply depots stocked in advance, wagon trains shuttling to the army — frees the army from the countryside's calendar and lets it operate in winter, in poor country, in enemy territory already eaten bare. But wagons are slow, their teams eat the cargo's margin, and the army becomes tethered: it can only move as far from its magazines as the shuttle can reach, and its line of supply is a target. The great magazine systems of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries made warfare methodical, siege-centered, and slow, because that is what the logistics could support.

Living off the land cuts the tether. The army requisitions or buys food and fodder where it stands, marches faster and farther, and can maneuver without a wagon train's tail. Napoleon systematized this into a strategic advantage: his armies dispersed to forage across a broad front, then concentrated to fight, moving at speeds magazine-bound opponents couldn't match. But the method consumes its own fuel — a district feeds an army for days, not weeks, so the army must keep moving or starve; it fails in poor, sparse, or scorched country (the retreat from Russia is the terminal case, where vast distances, thin agriculture, and winter annihilated the system); and it alienates the population whose food is being taken, which matters when occupation rather than passage is the goal.

The professional solution, when states could afford it, was hybrid: magazines and railways (later) for the base load, local purchase and requisition for the margin. The enduring lesson is that 'living off the land' is not the absence of a supply system — it is a supply system that eats geography instead of stores, with all the constraints geography imposes.
Pull it together for me: if you had to name the single deepest limit on pre-modern warfare — not weapons, not generalship — what is it?

Radius. Almost every constraint we have traced — fodder, water, the harvest calendar, the wagon team's appetite, the magazine's tether — expresses itself as a limit on how far force can be projected from its base of supply, and for how long it can stay there. A pre-modern army was not really a body of men; it was a daily consumption of a hundred tonnes or more that had to be assembled, every day, at a moving point on the map. The further the point from navigable water and stocked magazines, the more the supply system consumed itself delivering. Empires solved this with infrastructure — Rome's roads and granaries, China's canals — and the effective borders of pre-modern states sit suspiciously close to the lines where that infrastructure gave out.

This is why the famous aphorism of the field — that amateurs talk tactics while professionals talk logistics — survives even though its attribution is genuinely murky (it is usually credited to various American generals of the Second World War era, and no one has produced a solid source). The saying is true regardless of who said it: weapons decide engagements, but supply decides which engagements can be offered at all. Hannibal could win Cannae and still lose the war, because Rome's supply of men and grain, rooted in Italy's farms and its alliance system, outlasted his genius. The brilliant campaign far from base is a burning candle — spectacular, and on a timer.

When the constraint finally broke, it broke from outside warfare: steamships, railways, canning, and refrigeration industrialized supply in the nineteenth century, and operational radius expanded accordingly — bringing its own new horrors of scale. But for the thousands of years before, war's map was drawn by the stomach.

Lots of ancient and medieval public works were built with 'labor taxes' instead of money. Make that concrete: a district of 300 households owes the state 12 days of labor per household per year. How many labor-days does the state command, and what could that actually build?
The total labor the tax delivers — households times days owed:

The district owes 3600 labor-days a year.

Spend it mentally. A few thousand labor-days, applied in the agricultural off-season when the tax was usually levied, is a few kilometres of road grading, a stretch of canal dredging, a section of dike repair, a modest fortification — real infrastructure, built without a single coin changing hands. This is the corvée, and it was the default construction budget of most pre-modern states, from Egyptian dike crews to the French corvée royale that maintained (and embittered opinion against) the roads of the old regime.

Labor taxation solves a specific problem: the state needs work done in an economy where most people have no money to tax. Days are the one asset every household holds. It also has characteristic pathologies. The work arrives when the state calls it, not when the project needs it; the workers arrive with their own tools and food, at the season the state chooses — and if the call comes at harvest, the tax destroys the crop it was meant to be paid from. It is also brutally uneven: a money tax can be scaled to wealth, but a day of the poor man's labor is worth exactly a day, and he can spare it least.

States monetized labor dues as soon as their economies could support it — letting households commute days into cash and hiring workers with the proceeds — and the commutation was usually popular, which tells you how the tax was experienced. The corvée is a reminder that 'taxation' does not mean money. It means the state taking a share of the society's product, and labor was the original currency it took it in.
Slavery existed in many past societies, but I get the sense it wasn't one uniform thing. How did its forms actually differ?

It varied enormously, and the variation matters — though variation is not exculpation: every form rested on coercion and the legal treatment of a person as property or as bound. The main axes of difference were these. Source: war captives (the great supplier of the ancient world), birth into slave status, debt bondage (enslavement for unpaid debt — a major source in early societies, and repeatedly restricted or abolished precisely because it consumed citizens: Solon's Athens banned it for Athenians), judicial punishment, and organized slave trading. Function: mining and plantation labor at one extreme — the silver mines of Laurion and later the Caribbean sugar plantations were places of mass death — through agricultural estates, domestic service, skilled crafts, administration, and even banking and tutoring in Greek and Roman households, where an educated slave might live a materially comfortable life while remaining legally a thing.

Legal personhood differed. Roman law treated the slave as property with almost no standing, yet Roman practice developed manumission on a large scale — freed slaves became citizens, and their descendants were unmarked, which made Roman slavery brutal but unusually permeable. In many African and Asian systems, enslaved people could be absorbed over generations into kin groups, hold property, or rise in royal service; in the Atlantic system that developed after 1500, slavery became hereditary, racialized, and legally sealed in a way historians regard as distinctive in its totality — status inherited through the mother, manumission restricted, and an ideology of race built to justify permanence.

Scale differed too: slaves were a large share of the population in classical Athens and Roman Italy and in the plantation Americas, a smaller presence in many other agrarian societies where peasants, tenants, and corvée labor did the heavy work instead. The honest summary is that 'slavery' names a family of institutions united by coerced, alienable labor and legal unfreedom, differing in lethality, permeability, and economic role — and the differences explain both how each system functioned and how each was eventually attacked.
How did apprenticeship actually work as a contract? It sounds like education, employment, and a loan all at once.

That is exactly what it was — a bundled contract solving three problems that a poor, pre-modern economy could not solve separately. A master craftsman had skill that took years to transmit and no school to transmit it in. A family had a child who needed a trade and could not pay tuition up front. The indenture bound them: typically the parents paid a premium (a lump sum, scaled to the trade's prestige — high for goldsmiths and apothecaries, low for rough trades), and the master undertook to feed, house, clothe, discipline, and — the operative clause — teach the apprentice the 'art and mystery' of the craft over a term of years, seven being conventional in England. The apprentice undertook to serve, obey, keep the master's secrets, and not marry, trade on his own account, or absent himself.

The economics are precise. In the early years the apprentice's labor is worth less than his keep — the master is investing. In the later years his labor exceeds his keep — the family is repaid. The premium balances the risk that the boy runs away just as he becomes valuable, which is why runaway apprentices were pursued and why the indenture was a court-enforceable document, often registered with the guild or town. The guild's role was to police the market: limiting how many apprentices a master could take (protecting both training quality and future masters' earnings), and examining the finished product — the masterpiece — before admission to mastership.

The system reproduced more than skill. It reproduced the craft's social order: masters' sons got easier terms, outsiders paid more, and in many trades women were formally excluded even where they demonstrably did the work. Apprenticeship was the era's education finance, vocational school, and employment law in a single parchment — efficient, enforceable, and rigged in favor of those already inside.
What was the 'putting-out system'? I've seen it described as a factory without a building.

The description is exact. In putting-out (also called the domestic system), a merchant-entrepreneur owned the materials and the market, but not the workplace. He bought raw material — wool, flax, iron blanks — and distributed it to rural households, each performing one stage: spinning, weaving, nail-making, stocking-knitting. He collected the product at each stage, moved it to the next cottage, paid piece rates, and sold the finished cloth or hardware in distant markets his workers would never see. The workers owned their tools — the wheel, the loom in the cottage's best room — worked their own hours, and folded production around farming and childcare.

For centuries this was not a transitional curiosity but the dominant organization of European textile and metal production, and it had real advantages: no factory to build, no fixed wage bill, labor drawn from the countryside's underemployed margins, and output expandable by adding cottages. Its defects were the mirror of its looseness. The merchant could not supervise: materials were embezzled (workers kept back yarn and made up weight with moisture and worse — a whole vocabulary of fraud grew up), quality varied invisibly until the cloth reached the buyer, and coordinating stages across scattered cottages was slow. The merchant's capital spent much of its life as materials sitting in other people's houses.

Factories won, where and when they did, first on supervision and power, not on machinery alone: one roof let an employer watch the work, enforce hours and quality, and then exploit water and steam power that a cottage could not house. The transition was uneven and contested — handloom weavers persisted, and suffered terribly, for decades alongside the mills. But the putting-out system is the proof that industrial production was an organizational invention before it was a mechanical one: the factory's first innovation was gathering, not steam.
When I read tax lists and guild rolls from past centuries, women are nearly invisible. Were women not working, or is the record lying?

The record is not lying exactly; it is answering a different question than the one you are asking. Tax lists enumerate heads of household liable for tax — overwhelmingly men by legal construction. Guild rolls enumerate masters — a status formally closed to most women in most towns. The documents were built to track fiscal and corporate persons, and women, like children and servants, were filed inside a male-headed household. Absence from these lists is evidence about the lists.

Against the grain of other records — court cases, wills, inventories, church accounts, coroners' rolls — a different economy appears. Women dominate the recorded brewing trade in many late medieval English towns (the brewsters), until capital requirements and licensing pushed them out as brewing industrialized. Spinning was so thoroughly women's work that 'spinster' became the legal word for an unmarried woman. Dairying, poultry, market retailing, midwifery, laundry, and much of the food trades ran on women's labor, and widows routinely continued workshops — guild rules often explicitly allowed a widow to carry on her husband's trade and train apprentices, which quietly concedes that she knew it.

The methodological lesson generalizes: every source class has a designed blindness, and the historian's craft is to triangulate around it. The economy that tax lists describe — male, propertied, corporate — existed. So did the economy of unwaged, casual, seasonal, and household production that fed and clothed everyone, and women's work was concentrated precisely in the sectors the fiscal record was not built to see. When a source seems to show that some group did nothing, the first question is what the source was for.

Medieval people seem to have had an enormous number of holy days. Suppose a region keeps 52 Sundays plus 38 saints' days and festivals as non-working days in a year. What share of the year is that, and what did all those holidays actually do economically?

Their share of the year, as a percentage:

That is 90 days — 24.6575% of the year, very nearly a quarter of it, before you count local feasts, fairs, and the days lost to weather.

Treat the festival calendar as labor regulation, because that is one of the things it was. In a world without weekends as a concept — the two-day weekend is a twentieth-century artifact — the Church's calendar was the mechanism that limited the working year, and it did so with an authority no employer or lord could easily override, because working on a feast day was a sin, not just a contract breach. Lords disliked the lost labor and said so in their complaints; peasants defended the days fiercely, and they were among the things at stake in rural revolts.

The days were not idle in the economic sense either. Feast days were when fairs and markets met, when hiring was done (many labor contracts ran from one great feast to another), when dues were paid, marriages made, and news exchanged. The calendar was a coordination system: everyone resting on the same day is what makes a market, a court day, or a festival possible at all.

Two cautions belong with the arithmetic. The number of feast days varied widely by place and century — the figure here is a plausible composed case, and real calendars ranged from fewer to considerably more. And enforcement was uneven: hay harvest waits for no saint. The calendar set the aspiration and the negotiating baseline. But even discounted, the pre-modern working year was structured by religion in a way that makes modern arguments about 'how much people worked' mostly arguments about this calendar.
Who were journeymen, exactly? They seem to sit between apprentices and masters, and they had their own organizations, which seems unusual.

The journeyman — from the French journée, a day's work — was a man who had completed his apprenticeship and been freed of it, but was not yet a master: he owned his skill and his tools, sold his labor by the day or the piece, and did not own a workshop or the right to take apprentices. In the guild ideal this was a waiting room: save money, make your masterpiece, marry (often a master's daughter or widow, which greased the wheels), pay the fees, and rise. In practice, from the later Middle Ages onward, masterships in many towns became restricted — higher fees, limited numbers, preference for masters' sons — and the waiting room became a permanent condition for a large class of skilled men. That blockage is one of the deep sources of early labor conflict.

Journeymen responded with organization of their own: compagnonnages in France, Gesellenverbände in Germany — brotherhoods with their own rituals, funds, hostels, and the institution of the tramping years (the Wanderjahre), in which a journeyman travelled from town to town working under different masters. The tramping system spread techniques across Europe on foot, and it gave journeymen something like a labor market with a network: news of which towns were hiring, which masters were tyrants, which towns were 'closed' in a dispute.

And they struck. Journeymen's combinations — illegal almost everywhere, persistent anyway — withheld labor, enforced boycotts of struck workshops, and fought masters over wages and over the creeping use of unfree, unapprenticed labor. Historians of labor treat these associations as a genuine prehistory of trade unionism: not unions in the modern legal sense, but durable, self-governing workers' organizations built inside the shell of the guild system that had ceased to promote them.
Sumptuary laws — rules about who could wear silk, fur, certain colors — seem absurdly petty for governments to bother with. Why did they keep passing them?

Because clothing was a public language, and the laws were trying to control what could be said in it. In a society ordered by rank, dress announced status instantly, at a distance, to strangers: the fur, the fabric, the cut, the number of servants in livery. Sumptuary legislation — which appears from Rome through medieval and early modern Europe to Tokugawa Japan — typically reserved specific materials and styles to specific ranks, and its stated motives mixed several anxieties: moral (luxury corrupts), economic (spending on imported silk drains bullion; England repeatedly tried to protect its wool trade this way), and above all hierarchical — horror at the spectacle of a merchant's wife out-dressing a lord's.

That last anxiety is the tell. Sumptuary laws multiply exactly when societies get richer and ranks get blurry — when new money can buy the old signals. The laws are therefore evidence, whatever their framers intended, of social mobility happening faster than the hierarchy could absorb. A perfectly frozen society would not need them.

They also mostly failed, and the failure is documented in the repetition: a law reissued every generation for three hundred years is a law being broken for three hundred years. Enforcement against fashion, conducted by the same elites who loved display, was never going to win. Historians read sumptuary laws the way they read all prescriptive sources — as a map of what authorities feared, which is often more informative than what they achieved. The petty detail is the point: a state that legislates sleeve widths is a state that believes the social order is legible, visible, and worth defending at the level of cloth.
What did serfdom actually require of a serf day to day? I want the mechanics, not just 'they were unfree.'

The unfreedom was a bundle of specific obligations and disabilities, and the bundle varied — but its standard contents in medieval Europe ran like this. The serf held land from a lord and owed labor services on the lord's own farm (the demesne): classically week-work of two or three days a week, plus extra 'boon-work' at harvest, when the whole village turned out and was fed by the lord for the day. He owed dues in kind or cash — a share of grain, hens at Christmas, eggs at Easter, in the homely detail the manor court rolls record. He had to grind his corn at the lord's mill and bake in the lord's oven, paying for the privilege (the banalités in France) — monopolies that made the lord's infrastructure a tax on daily life. He could not leave the manor without permission, could not marry outside it without a fine (merchet), owed a payment when his holding passed to his heir (heriot — often his best beast), and was judged in the lord's court.

Two counterweights kept the system from being simple slavery. Custom protected the serf's own holding: the lord could not lawfully evict him or raise dues beyond 'the custom of the manor,' and the court rolls that record his obligations also record his rights — serfs sued in the manor court and sometimes won. And flight was a real option with a famous legal edge: in many German towns the rule ran that town air makes free — a serf who lived unclaimed in a chartered town for a year and a day was free of his lord. Lords hated it; towns thrived on it.

Serfdom decayed at different speeds — in Western Europe largely dissolving into rent-paying tenancy by the late Middle Ages, in Eastern Europe intensifying into the 'second serfdom' as grain exports made coerced labor profitable. Same word, opposite trajectories, which is why the mechanics matter more than the label: what was owed, to whom, enforced how, and what the exits were.
A historian's claim I half-remember: before factories, people didn't really experience 'work time' the way we do. Is that a real argument or a romantic exaggeration?

It is a real argument — E. P. Thompson's, in a famous 1967 essay on time and work-discipline — and it is more specific than the romantic version. Thompson's claim is that pre-industrial work was predominantly task-oriented: the working day was structured by the job to be done and by natural markers — daylight, tides, the cow's udder, the harvest's ripeness. Fishing, farming, and craft work have their own necessary rhythms, with bursts of intensity (harvest, a boat to catch) alternating with slack that looks like idleness to a factory inspector. Time was noticed, but it was not the employer's property, measured in units and bought by the hour; where time reckoning existed it was coarse — the canonical hours of prayer, the market bell.

Industrial capitalism, Thompson argued, required a different time sense to be installed in the workforce: the clock as supervisor, the working day as a uniform block sold to an employer, punctuality as a moral virtue, and the sharp modern boundary between 'work' and 'life' — the employer's time versus your own. Installing it took generations of bells, fines, schools, and sermons against 'time-wasting,' which is itself evidence that the older orientation was real and resistant.

The exaggerations to avoid: pre-modern people were not timeless innocents — monasteries ran on precise prayer schedules centuries earlier (the canonical hours are a time-discipline), towns rang work bells, and contracts specified days. Nor was task-orientation gentle: harvest labor could be fourteen hours of desperation. The defensible claim is about the default unit of work — the task versus the hour — and about whose clock governed. When the hour became the commodity, work felt different from the inside, and Thompson's essay remains the starting point for understanding why the factory whistle was experienced as a kind of conquest.
Writing is supposed to have been invented for literature or religion, but I've heard it actually started as accounting. What's the evidence?

The earliest evidence we have points to bookkeeping, and it comes with a plausible mechanism attached. In Mesopotamia, long before full writing, people tracked goods with small clay tokens — cones, spheres, discs — each shape standing for a commodity: a sheep, a jar of oil, a measure of grain. Tokens were sealed inside clay envelopes for transactions, with marks pressed on the outside to say what was inside; in time the marks made the tokens redundant, and the marks became signs pressed into flat tablets. Denise Schmandt-Besserat built the influential version of this theory, and while specialists debate details of the token-to-sign mapping, the broad picture is widely accepted: the first tablets, from Uruk around 3400–3300 BCE, are overwhelmingly administrative — ration lists, livestock accounts, labor records, land and tax notes. Literature, letters, and royal inscriptions come later.

Egypt's earliest writing tells a similar story of labels, tags, and accounts attached to goods and administration. And the pattern repeats independently: in China, the earliest surviving writing (oracle bones) serves royal divination and record; in Mesoamerica, the earliest scripts are entangled with calendars and royal accounting of tribute and time.

It makes functional sense. Speech handles the sacred and the memorable — myth and law carry themselves in trained memory and ritual. What unaided memory cannot do is hold ten thousand small obligations: who delivered what, who owes whom, what the storehouse contains. Writing was invented where the numbers outgrew the clerks' heads. The poem was an afterthought of the ledger — which is also why so much of what we know about the earliest societies comes from their accounts.
Why do historians make such a fuss about archives and tax registers? Aren't they the driest sources imaginable?

They are the driest and the most powerful, because a tax register is a state's description of its own society, made for use rather than for posterity — and therefore honest in ways chronicles never are. To tax people you must find them, name them, classify them, and value what they have. The Domesday Book of 1086 is the famous case: William the Conqueror's commissioners recorded, manor by manor, who held the land, how many ploughs, mills, fisheries, and tenants it had, and what it was worth in 1066 and in 1086 — an audit of a conquered kingdom so thorough that its nickname means judgment day, because there was no appeal from it. Nine centuries later it is still the foundation for studying eleventh-century England's economy, settlement by settlement.

The archive's power runs forward as well as backward. A state that keeps registers can tax next year on last year's knowledge, can prove claims, can conscript by list, can detect the village that has been under-reporting for a decade. Losing the records is losing the claims — conquerors and rebels alike have burned archives deliberately, because the archive is the state's memory and its weapon. Conversely, subjects hid from registers: evasion, under-declaration, and flight from the census are permanent features of the record, and the historian reads the register knowing it shows the society as the taxman could see it, not as it was.

So the fuss is justified. Chronicles tell you what a society said about itself; registers tell you what it could count. For the history of ordinary life — landholding, family size, prices, crops — the counting is usually worth more.

How expensive was a book before printing, in terms of labor? Take a substantial manuscript of 800 pages and a scribe who can produce about 3 good pages of text a day. How long does one copy take? And there's a claim that a single Bible needed the skins of a couple of hundred animals — is that the right ballpark?
Days of scribal labor for one copy:

One copy takes about 266.6667 working days of skilled scribal labor — the better part of a year, before ruling the pages, correcting, rubricating, illustrating, and binding.

And yes, the animal figure is the right ballpark for a large parchment Bible: estimates commonly run to the skins of roughly 200 to 300 sheep or calves for a single great pandect Bible, which is why the great early Bibles were institutional treasures, not personal possessions. Add the two together — a flock's worth of skins and a year of a trained man's life — and a book before printing was a capital asset on the scale of a house. Monasteries lent books against pledges of equal value; university students rented exemplars quire by quire to copy what they needed; books appear in wills, were chained to lecterns in libraries, and were stolen with the seriousness due to livestock.

The economics shaped the content. When every copy costs a year, copying is triage: texts survive because institution after institution judged them worth a year. The copying bottleneck is thus also a filter on everything we can know — the works of antiquity that reached us are the ones that kept winning that judgment, century after century, in a world where letting a text lapse for one generation could extinguish it.

What did printing actually do to the price of a book? Give me a sense of scale with round numbers: say a manuscript copy of a work cost around 300 units of money in the mid-fifteenth century, and a printed copy of a comparable work cost around 30 units a few decades later. What's the fall, in percent?
The price fall as a percentage of the manuscript price:

That is a 90% fall — the book at a tenth of its former price.

The specific figures here are illustrative round numbers, but they are in the range historians cite for the first print generations: the cost collapse was of an order of magnitude, not a percentage improvement, and it kept compounding as presses, paper mills, and distribution scaled up through the sixteenth century. The mechanism is the shift of cost from the copy to the edition. A scribe's price is per copy, forever. A printer's costs are front-loaded — type, composition, presswork for the run — and each additional copy costs little more than paper and press time. Print runs of a few hundred to over a thousand copies turned the book from a bespoke commission into a manufactured good with a market price.

The consequences cascade. Cheaper books meant more readers; more readers meant it paid to print in vernacular languages, for lay audiences, on new subjects — news, how-to, entertainment — that no patron would have commissioned in manuscript. It meant identical copies, which made citation, correction, and cumulative scholarship possible in a new way: an error could be identified in 'the' text because everyone had the same one. And it broke the monastery's and the university's monopoly on textual storage. Societies had stored knowledge in scarce, guarded copies for millennia; within two generations of Gutenberg, storage was cheap and guarding was futile. Every information revolution since has rhymed with that one.
Why would a calendar be a political instrument? It's just a way of counting days.

Because whoever sets the calendar decides when everything happens — when taxes fall due, when rents are paid, when festivals and fasts occur, when courts sit, when armies muster, and which saints and rulers get commemorated in the year's rhythm. A calendar is an operating system for a society's time, and reforming it is an assertion of sovereignty.

The Roman case is the template. Julius Caesar's reform of 45 BCE replaced a lunar calendar that priests had manipulated — inserting or withholding intercalary months for political advantage — with a clean solar year; it was an act of state rationalization, and it carried his name (July) into every subsequent year. Augustus took August. The Gregorian reform of 1582 shows the confessional edge: Pope Gregory XIII corrected the drift (the calendar had wandered ten days from the equinox) and Catholic states adopted at once, while Protestant and Orthodox countries refused a pope's calendar for generations — Britain and its colonies waited until 1752, Russia until 1918, by which time the gap was thirteen days. For centuries, neighboring countries literally lived on different dates, and letters were double-dated to cope.

Revolutionaries understand the stakes instinctively. The French Republic abolished the Christian calendar in 1793 and imposed its own — ten-day weeks, renamed months, Year One — precisely to break the Church's grip on time; it lasted twelve years before Napoleon restored the old reckoning, because a calendar everyone else rejects is a tax on every interaction. The lesson across all three cases: a calendar reform succeeds only when the reformer's power is great enough to make the whole society switch its habits at once. Counting days is never just counting days.
What is a cadastre, and why would measuring fields be an act of power?

A cadastre is a systematic survey and register of land: who holds each parcel, its boundaries, its quality, and its assessed value for tax. It sounds like paperwork. It is better understood as the state learning to see its territory — and what the state can see, it can tax, conscript against, adjudicate, and confiscate.

The power shows in what a survey reveals. Customary landholding is a tangle: overlapping rights, common grazing, plots held by usage no document mentions, land quietly cleared and farmed off the register. A cadastral survey forces all of it into parcels with owners and values. Concealed land appears — and with it, concealed tax liability; historians of several empires note that surveys were dreaded and sometimes resisted violently, because measurement is taxation in embryo. The Domesday inquiry frightened England in 1086 for exactly this reason. Napoleon's cadastre, the Austrian and later colonial surveys, and the great land settlements of British India all redrew what the state could extract, and India's settlements also hardened fluid customary rights into fixed ownership, with consequences — land becoming saleable, mortgageable, losable — that ran for generations.

Maps are the cadastre's visible half. Roman centuriation — the grid of surveyed allotments imposed on conquered land — is still legible from the air in parts of Italy and North Africa two thousand years later: the survey was that durable an intervention. And the instrument cuts both ways, which is the subtle part: once rights are registered, holders can defend them against the state itself, waving the register in court. Legibility empowers the taxman and the taxpayer in the same act, which is why land registration remains politically charged wherever it is introduced.
Were there real libraries in the ancient world, or is 'the Library of Alexandria' mostly a legend that grew?

Real libraries existed, in several civilizations, though the numbers attached to Alexandria grew in the telling. The oldest well-documented case is Ashurbanipal's library at Nineveh in the seventh century BCE: a royal collection of clay tablets — tens of thousands survive — systematically gathered, copied, and catalogued, covering omens, medicine, epics, and dictionaries. It was a state information project, and its baked tablets survived the fire that destroyed the palace precisely because they were clay.

Alexandria's library, founded under the early Ptolemies in the third century BCE, was the largest ancient attempt at universal collection: a research institute (the Mouseion) with a book-buying and copying operation that, ancient sources claim, even confiscated books from ships in harbor, copied them, and returned the copies. The scroll counts in ancient sources range wildly — into the hundreds of thousands — and modern scholars treat them as unreliable, partly because 'scroll' and 'work' are not the same unit (a single long work fills many scrolls). What is not legend is the institution's function: it concentrated scholars, texts, and royal money in one place, and the scholarship it produced — editing Homer, Euclid's Elements, Eratosthenes' measurement of the Earth — is documented in the works themselves.

Its end was likewise slower and duller than the legend of a single fire: decline by funding cuts, purges of scholars, partial fires (Caesar's harbor fire in 48 BCE damaged book stores, though how much is disputed), and the long attrition of a pagan institution in a Christianizing empire. The medieval chained library is the honest comparison for scale: a great cathedral library might hold a few hundred volumes, each one a capital asset, chained because a single book could be worth a farm. Ancient libraries were real; they were just small, fragile, and mortal in ways print made obsolete.
Before writing was common, how did societies remember long texts and important information? I don't fully believe the 'oral tradition' answer — human memory seems too fallible.

Your skepticism is healthy: unaided casual memory is fallible. Trained memory in oral cultures is a different instrument, and it used several technologies of the mind. The first is form: epic poetry in oral traditions is composed in meter with formulaic phrases — Homer's 'wine-dark sea' and 'swift-footed Achilles' are not decoration but building blocks, prefabricated chunks that fit the line and let a singer compose and recall thousands of lines. Milman Parry and Albert Lord demonstrated this by recording South Slavic epic singers in the twentieth century producing poems of epic length by exactly this method. Verse itself — rhythm and rhyme — is error-correction: a wrong word breaks the meter and announces itself.

The second is architecture: the method of loci, attributed in legend to Simonides, attaches items to places in a memorized building and retrieves them by walking through it — memory athletes still use it, because spatial memory is far stronger than list memory. The third is social distribution: in many societies, memory was a profession and a public act — genealogists, praise-singers, lawspeakers (Iceland's recited his law at the assembly), and ritual specialists whose performances were witnessed and corrected by audiences who also knew the material. An oral text is not stored in one skull; it is stored in a community's redundancy.

The honest limits: oral transmission preserves structure, story, law, and lineage superbly, and exact wording and statistics poorly — traditions reshape themselves toward present needs, telescoping generations and updating heroes. Historians treat oral sources as strong evidence for what a society valued and remembered about itself, and weaker evidence for dates and numbers. Writing did not replace a broken system; it replaced a system with different strengths — and the two ran in parallel for most of history.
Roman numerals are famously painful for arithmetic. What did people actually compute with before Hindu-Arabic numerals took over in Europe?

With their hands and with hardware — the numerals were for recording, the computing happened elsewhere. The standard instrument was the counting board or abacus: a board with lines or a frame with beads, on which counters (calculi — pebbles, the root of 'calculate') were placed in columns for units, tens, hundreds. You computed by moving counters, and you wrote down only the result, in Roman numerals, for the record. Skilled reckoners were fast; the Exchequer's own accounting in England was done on a checkered cloth (the 'exchequer' is literally the counting table) with counters and tallies, into the early modern period.

Hindu-Arabic numerals changed the location of computation: with place value and a zero, the written symbols themselves became the machine — pen-and-paper algorithms for multiplication and division became possible, teachable, and checkable. Fibonacci's Liber Abaci of 1202 is the great transmission document, arguing the business case to Italian merchants: the new numerals made interest, currency conversion, and partnership shares computable on paper by one man instead of by specialists with boards. Adoption was still slow — two centuries and more of coexistence — because the old system had institutional mass: guilds of reckoners, legal suspicion of easily altered Arabic figures (Florence's bankers' guild banned them in bookkeeping in 1299, partly over forgery risk), and the sheer cost of retraining.

The episode is a clean case of a notation being a technology. Nothing about the underlying arithmetic changed; what changed was the cost of doing it, and with the cost, who could do it and how much of it a society could afford. Double-entry bookkeeping, printed arithmetic books, and eventually the whole quantitative style of modern commerce ride on that notational shift.
It sometimes seems like ancient knowledge was constantly on the verge of being lost. Was preservation really that precarious?

Yes — and it helps to think of knowledge in a manuscript world as a stock that decays unless it is actively maintained. Every text existed in a small number of physical copies, each copy combustible, edible by worms and mold, and expensive to replace — a year of a scribe's labor for a large work. A text survived a century only if someone, in that century, paid to recopy it. Preservation was not a state but a subscription, renewed copy by copy, and the subscription lapsed for most of what was written: of the plays, histories, and poems antiquity produced, we have a small fraction — for some authors a tenth, for many nothing but titles quoted by others.

The losses were therefore mostly not bonfires. They were failures to recopy: a library's funding cut, a monastery's dissolution, a language dying (a text in a script no one reads is already lost), a shift of medium — the transition from scroll to codex, and later from papyrus to parchment, each stranded works nobody bothered to transcribe into the new format. The famous burnings — Alexandria above all — are better understood as episodes in a long attrition than as its main cause.

Two consequences follow. First, what survives is selected: school texts, scripture, law, and useful medicine were recopied relentlessly; the frivolous, the heretical, and the merely old were let go — our picture of antiquity is drawn from what a thousand years of copyists judged worth a year's labor. Second, preservation had geography: texts that reached multiple centers — monasteries across Europe, the translation movement that carried Greek science into Arabic in Baghdad and back into Latin in Spain — acquired redundancy, and redundancy is what actually saves information. Knowledge in the manuscript age did not usually die by murder. It died by neglect, one unrenewed subscription at a time.
The Champagne fairs are described as the engine of medieval European trade. What did a fair actually do besides host a lot of buying and selling?

The buying and selling was almost the least of it. The fairs of Champagne — a cycle of six fairs rotating through four towns (Troyes, Provins, Lagny, Bar-sur-Aube) across the year — sat at the crossroads between the cloth towns of Flanders and the Italian cities, protected by the counts of Champagne, whose safe-conducts and fair courts made the route worth taking. A fair ran in regulated phases: entry and setup, the cloth fair, the leather and goods fair, and finally the settlement — and the settlement phase is where the fair became a bank.

Merchants arrived having bought and sold on credit all season, owing and owed in a web that spanned Europe. At the fair's settlement days, debts were presented, offset against each other — a practice the Italians called scontration — and only the net balances were paid in coin or carried forward as new credit to the next fair. A merchant could clear a season's obligations across a dozen counterparties by moving a fraction of the gross sum. The fairs thus functioned as a clearing house before banks existed to be one, and their letters and obligations circulated as credit instruments in their own right.

Add the rest of the bundle: a specialized court giving fast judgments between merchants (enforced by the sanction of exclusion from future fairs), standardized weights and inspected cloth, money-changers whose exchange tables linked the currencies of Europe, and the counts' protection making the whole apparatus credible. When the fairs declined in the fourteenth century, it was not because trade shrank — it was because the functions unbundled: Italian banks took the clearing, sea routes bypassed the land corridor, and royal taxation and war made Champagne a worse address. The fair is best understood as a periodic city of finance that assembled, did the continent's accounts, and dissolved — six times a year.

One camel-load costs 1200 coins to move. Loaded with grain, it earns 1000 — a loss of 200 coins before the merchant has fed himself. Loaded with silk, it earns 40000 coins against the same 1200 cost.

That is the entire economics of long-distance overland trade in one subtraction: transport cost is charged by weight and distance, so only goods whose value per kilogram towers over the transport cost can survive the journey. Grain, timber, and other bulk staples are effectively untransportable overland beyond a few hundred kilometres — their delivered price is all freight. What crosses deserts and mountain passes is the concentrated essence of value: silk, spices, gems, precious metals, dyes, fine glassware, medicines — luxuries, because only luxuries can pay the road.

Hence the shape of the famous trade routes. The Silk Road did not feed anybody; it dressed and seasoned the rich at both ends of Eurasia, and its cargoes passed through many hands, each adding a margin, which is why silk in Rome could cost what it did. Bulk goods moved by water or not at all. When you read that a caravan city grew rich, translate it as: the city taxed, guarded, watered, and re-sold a stream of goods each kilogram of which was worth a laborer's month. The camel's 200 kilograms is the filter that decided what 'world trade' could even consist of before steam.
What was the Hanseatic League? A country? A company? It seems to have acted like both.

Neither, exactly — it was a league of cities, and for about three centuries it behaved like a trade power without being a state. The Hansa grew out of associations of German merchants abroad and crystallized in the thirteenth century around Lübeck, whose law became the template for dozens of Baltic towns. At its height it linked, by most counts, well over a hundred towns from the Netherlands to Novgorod, but its skeleton was the four great Kontore — fortified trading stations abroad: the Steelyard in London, the German Wharf at Bergen, the Peterhof at Novgorod, and the settlement at Bruges.

What the league actually did was collective bargaining with geography. A single town's merchants could be robbed, taxed, or expelled by any prince; the Hansa could retaliate with an embargo, and an embargo by the league meant the herring, grain, timber, wax, and furs of the Baltic stopped moving — a weapon it used, successfully, against kings. It negotiated privileges (fixed tolls, legal protections, extraterritorial jurisdiction in its stations) as a bloc, standardized commercial practice among its members, and occasionally went to war as a bloc, defeating Denmark in the 1370s and dictating the Treaty of Stralsund.

Its decline shows its nature. It had no treasury, no standing fleet, no executive — its diets (Hansetage) issued decisions that member cities obeyed when convenient. As territorial states consolidated, as Dutch and English shipping competed, and as trade's center of gravity shifted to the Atlantic, the league's looseness became fatal: it could not tax, could not compel, could not adapt. The last diet met in 1669 with a handful of cities represented. The Hansa is the standing proof that trade networks can generate state-like power for centuries — and that without the fiscal core of a state, the power is borrowed against a world that eventually changes.
Port cities in the past seem to have been full of foreign merchants living in their own quarters. Why did trade need that kind of arrangement?

Because long-distance trade is a collision of incompatible systems, and the port city was where the collision was managed. A merchant arriving from another world brought foreign coin (of uncertain fineness), foreign weights and measures, foreign law, a foreign language, foreign gods, and no local credit or reputation. Every one of those mismatches is friction, and the entrepôt's job was to convert between systems: money-changers assayed and exchanged coin, official weighers certified quantities, brokers and interpreters (dragomans in the Ottoman world) bridged language and custom, and the port's courts offered foreigners a forum whose judgments both sides could predict.

The foreign quarter was the institutional form of that conversion. Venice's Fondaco dei Tedeschi housed German merchants under rules — they lived, stored, and traded in one supervised building; the fondaco system, and its Islamic-world counterpart the funduq or khan, combined warehouse, hostel, customs post, and surveillance. The host city gained control and tax; the foreigners gained security, legal standing, and each other's company and information. Similar structures recur everywhere trade crossed civilizational borders: the foreign concessions of Canton, the Armenian and Jewish merchant quarters of great ports, the Hansa's walled Kontore.

What the port city sold, in the end, was trust at a discount. Inland, a stranger's promise was worth little; in the entrepôt, institutions — the quarter, the brokers, the exchange, the court — manufactured enough trust for strangers to deal in bulk. Cities that manufactured it best (Venice, Amsterdam, Singapore in their turns) took the trade of continents. The quarter full of foreigners is not a curiosity of the pre-modern port; it is the visible machinery of its prosperity.

Britain's tea duty in the eighteenth century is the classic case: at one point the duty effectively raised the price of legal tea by about 25% over its base price, and smuggling was rampant. If tea's base cost is 100, what does the legal buyer pay, and how much room does that leave a smuggler who sells at the legal price's level but skips the duty?

The legal buyer pays 125; the smuggler's margin is 25 per unit — a fifth of the selling price — out of which he pays for fast boats, bribes, storage, and losses to seizure, and still, at eighteenth-century volumes, made fortunes.

The general law is that smuggling volume is a function of the tax wedge: the gap between the legal price and the untaxed cost is the smuggler's budget, and the bigger the wedge, the more enforcement he can afford to evade or corrupt. Tea is the cleanest historical demonstration because Britain ran the experiment in both directions. Duties on tea were pushed so high in the mid-eighteenth century — at points effectively above the 25% in our model, by some reckonings near or beyond the tea's own value — that historians estimate a majority, possibly a large majority, of the tea drunk in Britain had paid no duty. The East India Company, which held the legal monopoly, was being bankrupted by untaxed competition. Pitt's Commutation Act of 1784 slashed the duty to a small fraction, legal tea's price collapsed toward the smugglers', and the tea-smuggling trade withered within a few years — not because enforcement improved, but because the margin did.

The same arithmetic explains contraband in brandy, tobacco, salt (the French gabelle made salt smuggling — faux-saunage — a mass crime), and every modern taxed or banned good. Smugglers are not primarily a policing problem; they are a price signal with boats. Where you see flourishing smuggling, you are looking at a wedge someone set too wide.
The Dutch and English East India Companies had their own armies and made treaties. How can a company be a state?

By charter — that was the legal mechanism. When the Dutch Republic chartered the VOC in 1602 and England chartered the East India Company in 1600, the charters delegated slices of sovereignty to the company in its theater of operations: the right to wage war and make peace, conclude treaties with Asian rulers, build fortresses, administer justice over its servants and settlements, and in the Dutch case coin money. The states did this deliberately: they wanted Asian trade's profits without paying for Asian wars from the treasury, so they franchised the violence to a joint-stock corporation that could raise its own capital for it.

The results followed the incentives. The VOC, answerable to directors in Amsterdam months away by ship, built a territorial empire in the Indonesian archipelago, enforced a spice monopoly by methods that included the near-extermination of the Bandanese in 1621, and ran courts, taxes, and garrisons as a government that happened to pay dividends. The English Company, after winning at Plassey in 1757 and taking the diwani (revenue administration) of Bengal in 1765, became the tax-collecting ruler of tens of millions of Indians while remaining, in London, a corporation with shareholders and a stock price. The seams showed constantly: company servants enriching themselves, famines under company administration (Bengal 1770 was the scandal that forced Parliament's hand), and the British state progressively reasserting control — regulating acts, a governor-general answerable to London, and finally, after the rebellion of 1857, abolition of company rule altogether.

The company-state is not a quaint anomaly; it is what happens when a state outsources expansion to capital. The charter made sovereignty divisible and delegable, and the companies demonstrated both how effectively private organization could wield it and how badly the accountability worked when the governed had no claim on the governors and the shareholders were an ocean away. Modern arguments about chartered monopolies, private military companies, and corporate governance of infrastructure are, structurally, arguments the seventeenth century already had.
Something I never thought about: were weights and measures standardized in the past? Or did every town really have its own bushel?

Every town really could have its own bushel — and its own ell, rod, pound, and gallon, differing not only between countries but between neighboring towns and even between commodities in the same town (a measure for grain, another for ale). This was not mere sloppiness. Measures were property and policy: market tolls were taken in kind with the lord's measure, which had a suspicious tendency to be large when collecting and small when paying out — the heaped versus striked (levelled) measure was a perennial dispute, and biblical injunctions against 'divers measures' show the grievance is ancient. Local measures also embodied local custom and privilege, defended like any other right.

The costs were real: every long-distance transaction needed conversion, every conversion invited error and fraud, and merchants kept tables and employed specialists the way they later kept exchange tables for currencies. States pushed standardization for the usual reason — taxes and armies run better on uniform units — and towns kept official standards physically at the market cross or church door: standard bushels, ell-wands, and weights against which traders' measures could be checked. England's Magna Carta already demands uniform measures for wine, ale, and corn in 1215; the demand had to be repeated for six centuries.

Full standardization arrived only with the modern state's administrative reach, and its emblem is the metric system — a deliberate revolutionary project of the 1790s to replace the patchwork with units derived from nature and identical everywhere. That the patchwork survived into the nineteenth century, in the most commercial societies on earth, is a useful corrective: standardization is not a default of markets. It is a political achievement, usually imposed over the resistance of everyone whose local measure was a local advantage.
How did merchants handle the risk of shipping goods by sea before insurance companies existed? One wreck could ruin you.

They sliced the risk until no single loss could. The first technique was division: never put everything in one hull. Merchants split cargoes across several ships, and investors took fractional shares in multiple ventures rather than whole shares in one — the logic of the portfolio, practiced centuries before it was theorized. A related device was the commenda and its cousins: a sedentary investor supplied capital, a travelling partner supplied labor and risk of person, and profits split by a formula fixed in advance — risk-sharing as a contract type, found from medieval Italy to the Islamic qirad, whose resemblance is no coincidence.

The second technique embedded insurance inside credit. In a sea loan (bottomry, in its later name), a lender advanced money for a voyage at high interest, on the term that if the ship was lost, the debt died with it. The premium over ordinary interest was, in substance, an insurance premium — the lender was being paid to absorb the sea's risk. Roman and Greek practice had versions of this; medieval Italian ports refined it.

True marine insurance — a separate contract, a premium, an underwriter who takes the risk for a fee and nothing else — crystallized in the Italian ports in the fourteenth century and spread to Antwerp and London, where Lloyd's coffee house became its market. The sequence matters: insurance was the last piece, not the first. Merchants managed for millennia with diversification and risk-priced credit, and insurance proper appears when trade volumes and merchant wealth made a specialized risk market thick enough to sustain. Risk never stopped anyone trading; it just priced itself into every contract until it got a market of its own.
